ctx.x: home the following morning. So, we opened up with Chester Clark. They had dancers back in those days, cabaret dancers, and the dancers would sing to each table, before coming back on the floor and singing their last chorus. And they would keep the money, tips, rather, that they made in their hands and when they finished singing the would bring the money up to the bandleader and put it into a kitty.

That was the style of the cabarets back in that day. We found out that by working all night and sometimes early and late in the morning a -- that our salary would run for a week around about $20-$25, and sometimes $30.00 a week. Which wasn't too bad during that time, in the Depression. We worked there with Chester Clark's band all through the following year through the Christmas holidays. And we gave him our notice because we were offered a job -- Jeter and myself, decided to organize a band of our own and we was…

In the band we had A. G. Godley, the drummer; we Had Harry Sweets Edison, we had -- our reed section and we sent to Utica, New York, and got a fella named Goodson. His nickname was Serp, on the piano. And we -- on the bass we had an old gentleman, much older than us, that we had known back in the Alphonso Trent days, his days was [Nunu], I can't think of his

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had played with Jo Jones and Walter Page in St. Louis with a band called Jeter-Pillars, it was James Jeter and Hayes Pillars.

ctx.x: Yeah, because we never got to see each other too much anyway. Of course when I joined Count Basie’s band in 1938…when I first went to New York and joined Lucky Millinder’s band and Lucky had a good band and I enjoyed playing…he had Don Byas in the band, he had Charlie Shavers, Billy Kyle who later joined Louis Armstrong and…oh he had a good band, Walter Johnson was on drums, wonderful drummer. And some reason or the other, Lucky fired me for Dizzy and that’s when I went with Basie’s band because I had played with…

Before we get too far into Count Basie, one question before we leave your early background: you said your uncle had taught you the scales, the trumpet. How did you actually learn to read music, was that from him as well, or…?
